claim_afe7cc7b19317ee0.claim_text: Global data centers consumed approximately 415 TWh of electricity in 2024 (about 1.5% of world electricity consumption), with a regional split of US 45%, China 25%, Europe 15%, and data center electricity consumption grew ~12%/year since 2017 (over 4x the rate of total electricity consumption growth). STATUS=OBSERVED. AI_ATTRIBUTION=PARTIAL: IEA names AI as 'the most important driver of this growth, alongside growing demand for other digital services' but does not isolate AI's specific numeric share versus crypto/general cloud workloads.
claim_afe7cc7b19317ee0.scope: Global + US/China/Europe data center electricity consumption, 2024 level and 2017-2024 growth rate

claim_1d9458f4e7e2cf69.claim_text: IEA projects global data center electricity consumption could more than double to approximately 945 TWh by 2030 and approximately 1200 TWh by 2035, with the US representing by far the largest share of the projected increase; up to ~20% of planned data center projects could be at risk of delay due to grid bottlenecks if risks are not addressed. STATUS=FORECAST (explicitly IEA's own projection, not an observed value -- must never be merged with the 2024 observed 415 TWh figure as if both were measured facts). AI_ATTRIBUTION=PARTIAL, same basis as the 2024 figure.
claim_1d9458f4e7e2cf69.scope: IEA projected global data center electricity consumption, 2030 and 2035

claim_d170f52f567053e9.claim_text: Despite Google's hyperscale data centers reaching a power usage effectiveness (PUE) of approximately 1.1 (near the theoretical efficiency limit), Google's total energy consumption increased 3.7x from 2016 to 2022, per peer-reviewed modeling of general cloud computing (Meta/Google infrastructure). STATUS=OBSERVED (within the paper's own dataset). The authors interpret this as a Jevons-paradox dynamic: point-level efficiency gains do not by themselves reduce aggregate energy growth because demand elasticity and reinvestment expand system scale. AI_ATTRIBUTION=INDIRECT: this paper models general cloud computing, not AI-specific workloads, and is evidence against the 'efficiency alone will solve AI energy growth' framing rather than a direct AI electricity measurement.
claim_d170f52f567053e9.scope: Google/Meta hyperscale cloud energy consumption vs. PUE efficiency, 2016-2022

claim_5787125ab5f0110b.claim_text: Approximately 130 GW of capacity-eligible generation projects are stuck, unbuilt, in PJM's interconnection queue; GridLab estimates PJM customers could have saved approximately $3.5 billion in the 2026/27 delivery year had just 10% of queued projects been operational, and the 2026/2027 PJM capacity auction cleared at $16.1 billion, up 10% year over year. STATUS=OBSERVED for the queue size and auction price; ESTIMATED (counterfactual model) for the $3.5B savings figure. AI_ATTRIBUTION=PARTIAL: GridLab attributes PJM demand growth to 'data center additions and electrification' jointly, not AI specifically, and frames this explicitly as a generation/interconnection-queue supply shortage, not a transmission/distribution capacity bottleneck.
claim_5787125ab5f0110b.scope: PJM interconnection queue backlog and capacity auction price, US PJM region

claim_o1_lbnl_us_dc_2023.claim_text: US data centers consumed approximately 176 TWh of electricity in 2023 (about 4.4% of total US electricity consumption), up from 58 TWh in 2014; LBNL projects 325-580 TWh by 2028 (6.7-12% of US electricity). STATUS: 2023 figure is OBSERVED, 2028 figure is FORECAST (kept as separate claim fields, not merged). AI_ATTRIBUTION=PARTIAL: LBNL states growth since 2017 is 'largely due to the growth in AI servers' but the published summary does not disaggregate AI training vs. inference vs. general cloud/non-AI compute -- attribution is explicit-but-aggregate, matching the existing IEA claim's AI_ATTRIBUTION=PARTIAL pattern, not an independent granular breakdown.
claim_o1_lbnl_us_dc_2023.scope: US data center electricity consumption, LBNL/DOE 2024 US Data Center Energy Usage Report
claim_o1_lbnl_us_dc_2023.evidence_independence: ACADEMIC_RESEARCH (DOE-funded national lab report, not a corporate self-report)

forecast_fields.scenario: LBNL central range (low/high growth scenarios), not further named
forecast_fields.publisher: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory / US DOE

claim_o1_korea_capital_region_dc_demand.claim_text: Per KEPCO data presented at a Korean National Assembly audit (국정감사, cited by Rep. Lee So-young / 이소영 의원), contracted data-center electricity capacity requested nationwide through 2029 totals 14.7 GW, of which 13.5 GW (91.8%) is concentrated in the Seoul capital region (Seoul 3,237 MW/51 facilities, Gyeonggi 8,789 MW/118 facilities, Incheon 1,494 MW/13 facilities). KEPCO's 9th transmission/transformation facility plan reportedly warns that meeting 50% of new data-center demand in the capital region will be difficult due to supply-capacity shortages. AI_ATTRIBUTION=UNKNOWN/INDIRECT: source describes 'data center' (IDC) electricity demand broadly, not an AI-specific workload breakdown.
claim_o1_korea_capital_region_dc_demand.time_scope: FORECAST through 2029 (contracted capacity requests as of reporting date)
claim_o1_korea_capital_region_dc_demand.scope: Korean data center electricity demand geographic concentration
claim_o1_korea_capital_region_dc_demand.provenance: https://www.energydaily.co.kr/news/articleView.html?idxno=122062 (news report of National Assembly / KEPCO audit material); underlying primary data is KEPCO + National Assembly 국정감사 material, not independently fetched from KEPCO/국회 directly in this pass
claim_o1_korea_capital_region_dc_demand.evidence_independence: DERIVATIVE_REPORTING (news coverage of a primary government/public-utility data disclosure; the primary document itself -- the 국정감사 submission -- was NOT independently located or fetched in this pass, so this is recorded as NEWS/SECONDARY per the stated rule, not promoted to POLICY_RESEARCH)
claim_o1_korea_capital_region_dc_demand.rights_note: Public news reporting of government audit data -- no private/paywalled full text involved; safe for Public-facing output as metadata/summary.

claim_3ab07077d739a9a4.claim_text: Data centres consumed 22% of Ireland's metered electricity in 2024 (6,969 GWh), up from 6,335 GWh in 2023 (10% YoY increase) and from 5% of metered electricity in 2015. STATUS: OBSERVED (CSO official statistics), not AI-specific. AI_ATTRIBUTION=INDIRECT: a separate University College Cork academic study (Prof. Hannah Daly) argues AI-driven growth is contributing, but the CSO's own metered-electricity data does not disaggregate AI workload from general colocation/cloud/non-AI data center demand -- the 22% figure is all-data-center, not AI-isolated.
claim_3ab07077d739a9a4.scope: Ireland national metered electricity consumption by data centers, CSO Data Centres Metered Electricity Consumption survey 2024
claim_3ab07077d739a9a4.evidence_independence: PRIMARY_SOURCE (national statistics office, CSO) via DERIVATIVE_REPORTING summary -- CSO release itself not independently refetched this pass

claim_931b08c7ebfc9604.claim_text: The EU Energy Efficiency Directive (EU) 2023/1791, Article 12, requires data centres in the EU with installed IT power demand of at least 500 kW to report energy performance data annually (from September 2024) into a common European database, administered via the JRC/European Commission. STATUS: this is a POLICY ANNOUNCEMENT / REPORTING-OBLIGATION IN FORCE, NOT an observed reduction in energy use -- no claim is made here that the directive has changed aggregate EU data center electricity consumption; it only establishes a measurement regime. AI_ATTRIBUTION=NOT_APPLICABLE (the directive applies to all data centers, not AI-specific).
claim_931b08c7ebfc9604.scope: EU-wide data center energy reporting obligation under Energy Efficiency Directive Art.12
claim_931b08c7ebfc9604.provenance: https://interactdc.com/static/images/documents/JRC135926_01.pdf (JRC data center energy report referencing the EED Art.12 reporting scheme); context via https://www.iiea.com/blog/data-centres-in-ireland-the-state-of-play
claim_931b08c7ebfc9604.evidence_independence: PRIMARY_SOURCE (EU legislative text / JRC) -- directive text itself not independently fetched and read line-by-line this pass; classification kept conservative
claim_931b08c7ebfc9604.policy_classification: POLICY_ANNOUNCEMENT_REPORTING_OBLIGATION (NOT an observed effect/outcome; no post-implementation impact data found this pass)

claim_afe484e45964c605.claim_text: China's data center electricity consumption is estimated at roughly 100 TWh in 2024 (IEA estimate) to 200 TWh (Goldman Sachs estimate, as reported by Bloomberg), up from approximately 77 TWh in 2022 (cited to Chinese government figures), representing an estimated 0.9-2.7% of China's total electricity consumption depending on source. FORECAST: 400-600 TWh by 2030 (~200 MtCO2e associated emissions), per the same mixed government/analyst estimates -- range kept wide and attributed per-source because PRC government figures and Western analyst estimates diverge substantially. China's 'East Data West Computing' (东数西算) program, launched 2022, redirects non-real-time computing load to western provinces with larger renewable (solar/wind) capacity, aiming to address the geographic mismatch between renewable generation (concentrated in the north/west) and compute demand (concentrated in eastern coastal cities). AI_ATTRIBUTION=INDIRECT: sources attribute growth generically to 'AI and other technologies' without quantifying an AI-specific share.
claim_afe484e45964c605.scope: China national data center electricity consumption + East Data West Computing regional program
claim_afe484e45964c605.provenance: https://www.carbonbrief.org/explainer-how-china-is-managing-the-rising-energy-demand-from-data-centres (Carbon Brief, citing IEA, Goldman Sachs/Bloomberg, and Chinese State Council/government figures)
claim_afe484e45964c605.evidence_independence: DERIVATIVE_REPORTING / ACADEMIC_ANALYSIS -- Carbon Brief is a Western climate-policy analysis outlet; it cites but is not itself a primary Chinese government document. The underlying 77 TWh 2022 figure is attributed to Chinese government sources by Carbon Brief but was not independently located/fetched in a primary PRC government publication this pass -- so this claim is NOT tagged PRIMARY_SOURCE or POLICY_RESEARCH, only DERIVATIVE_REPORTING, consistent with the Korea claim's treatment.

claim_a11c5cb4c7c4c2d1.claim_text: Grid Strategies LLC's national load-growth reports ("Strategic Industries Surging: Driving US Power Demand", 2024, and "Power Demand Forecasts Revised Up for Third Year Running, Led by Data Centers", 2025) identify 'strategic industries' -- semiconductor fabs, battery/EV manufacturing, hydrogen, and LNG (i.e. reshoring/industrial-policy-driven manufacturing) -- as a driver of rising utility load forecasts named independently of, and alongside, data centers. STATUS=OBSERVED at the level of 'a named, non-AI industrial driver exists in utility planning data'; NOT a quantified TWh split versus data-center/AI demand (report body itself was not fetched in the originating pass, only report-title/summary level). This describes a co-occurring structural demand driver, not a finding that it disproves or displaces any AI-attributed demand growth. AI_ATTRIBUTION=NOT_APPLICABLE (manufacturing/reshoring load growth is a non-AI driver by construction; this claim says nothing about AI's share of demand).
claim_a11c5cb4c7c4c2d1.scope: US utility load-growth forecasts attributing a share of new demand to strategic/reshored manufacturing industries

claim_f5842e6162c8fefc.claim_text: Per IEA's Global EV Outlook 2025, global EV charging consumed approximately 180 TWh of electricity in 2024 (about 0.7% of final global electricity consumption), a 60% increase over 2023. STATUS=OBSERVED for the 2024 figure. FORECAST (IEA Stated Policies Scenario): EV electricity demand could grow more than fourfold to approximately 780 TWh by 2030 (about 2.5% of global electricity demand; over 4% in Europe, 3.6% in China) -- kept as a separate forecast field, never merged with the 2024 observed figure. No US-specific TWh figure was given in the fetched section. This is real, independent, non-AI electricity-demand growth (EV charging), roughly half the 2024 observed scale of global data center consumption (180 TWh vs. 415 TWh), and is NOT shown to explain any AI-specific or data-center-specific grid bottleneck (e.g. PJM interconnection delays) -- it is evidence of a parallel/co-driver demand source, not evidence against AI's contribution. AI_ATTRIBUTION=NOT_APPLICABLE (EV charging demand is a non-AI driver by construction; this claim says nothing about AI's share of demand).
claim_f5842e6162c8fefc.scope: Global (and EU/China) EV charging electricity consumption, 2024 observed and 2030 IEA Stated Policies Scenario forecast

claim_d641fb1790c3ef53.claim_text: Multiple independent EIA 'Today in Energy' notes (June heat wave increased electricity demand in the eastern and midwestern United States, https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=62410 ; Texas power grid met record-breaking demand for electricity during recent heat wave, https://www.eia.gov/todayinEnergy/detail.php?id=57240) and an Ember analysis ("Powering through the heat: how 2024 heatwaves reshaped electricity demand", https://ember-energy.org/latest-insights/powering-through-the-heat-how-2024-heatwaves-reshaped-electricity-demand/) document that 2024/2025 heat waves drove record or near-record PEAK electricity demand in ERCOT (Texas) and the Eastern Interconnection via air-conditioning load. STATUS=OBSERVED. This is a real, non-AI, weather-driven demand channel operating on PEAK/HOURLY timescales, not the multi-year annual TWh growth trend that the IEA/LBNL AI_ENERGY_INFRA claims track -- it is a genuine alternative explanation for PEAK LOAD STRESS episodes specifically, and must never be merged with annual-baseline electricity-growth claims as if they measured the same thing. AI_ATTRIBUTION=NOT_APPLICABLE (weather-driven peak demand is a non-AI driver by construction; this claim says nothing about AI's share of demand).
claim_d641fb1790c3ef53.scope: US (ERCOT/Eastern Interconnection) peak electricity demand during 2024-2025 heat waves

claim_b9370aa7d219d791.claim_text: The OECD AI Exposure Measure (built on AI Capability Indicators across nine cognitive/social/physical domains) finds occupations involving routine information processing, administrative work, and codifiable tasks have the highest AI exposure, while roles requiring contextual judgment, interpersonal understanding, and complex decision-making have the lowest exposure; the measure explicitly assesses exposure/capability-gap only, not actual job displacement, which the OECD states depends on adoption, regulation, organisational change and social choice.
claim_b9370aa7d219d791.scope: Occupational AI exposure (capability-gap methodology), not displacement

claim_4731da53eae6b843.claim_text: US BLS JOLTS report for August 2026 (released September 29, 2026) recorded job openings at 7.1 million (4.3% rate), hires at 5.2 million (3.3% rate), and total separations at 5.1 million (3.2% rate), each described by BLS as little changed/unchanged from the prior month.
claim_4731da53eae6b843.scope: US aggregate labor market flow data (JOLTS), no AI attribution in the release itself

claim_fe878b52922b46a4.claim_text: A field experiment (Brynjolfsson, Li, and Raymond, NBER Working Paper 31161, 2023) studying 5,179 customer support agents given a generative-AI conversational assistant found a 14% average increase in issues resolved per hour, with a 34% improvement for novice/low-skilled workers and minimal effect for experienced/highly skilled workers; this is a productivity (output-per-hour) finding, not evidence of employment or headcount change at the firm.
claim_fe878b52922b46a4.scope: Firm-level productivity effect of generative AI tool on customer support agents; NOT employment/headcount evidence
claim_fe878b52922b46a4.geographic_scope: US (single large US software firm call center, per paper)

claim_8fd5da8f27c9fc2b.claim_text: A Stanford SIEPR working paper (Brynjolfsson, Chandar, Chen, 'Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence', Aug 2025), using large-scale US payroll processor data, found early-career workers (ages 22-25) in the most AI-exposed occupations experienced an estimated 13% relative decline in employment since the widespread adoption of generative AI tools, compared to stable or growing employment for more experienced workers in the same occupations and for workers in less-exposed occupations; the paper reports adjustment occurring through employment levels rather than compensation, and attributes the pattern primarily to roles where AI automates (vs. augments) tasks.
claim_8fd5da8f27c9fc2b.scope: US labor market; early-career (ages 22-25) workers in high-AI-exposure occupations, since generative AI adoption (post-2022)

claim_30fdf98bc1a9c818.claim_text: Korea Development Institute (KDI) report '인공지능(AI)의 거시경제 영향 분석' (Analysis of AI's Macroeconomic Impact, released July 22, 2026) FORECASTS that over a 10-year horizon AI diffusion could raise Korea's total factor productivity by up to 3.5% (annual gains of roughly 0.15-0.35 percentage points), while projecting approximately 256,000 jobs per year could be displaced (about 2.1% of Korea's 2024 employed workforce), concentrated in mid-to-high-skill professional, administrative, and sales roles; separately, the report estimates 72% of occupations have some AI-automatable tasks today but only 1.4% of jobs (1.8% by revenue) are currently economically viable to automate immediately.
claim_30fdf98bc1a9c818.scope: Korea; national macroeconomic projection, 10-year horizon forecast -- NOT an observed/realized outcome

claim_8e305d0c30d23514.claim_text: A peer-reviewed study (Kauhanen & Rouvinen, 'Assessing Early Labour Market Effects of Generative AI: Evidence from Population Data', Applied Economics Letters, published online June 10, 2025, ETLA/Finland) using comprehensive Finnish wage-earner population data found NO statistically significant differences in wage or employment changes between more-exposed and less-exposed occupations in the two years following ChatGPT's November 2022 launch, in contrast to some online-labour-market-based studies; the authors note generative AI may simultaneously complement some tasks and substitute others in ways that have not yet produced a detectable net employment or wage effect at the national population level.
claim_8e305d0c30d23514.scope: Finland; national population-level wage/employment data by occupational AI-exposure, 2 years post-ChatGPT launch -- counterevidence to displacement hypothesis

claim_0da20db21fe1463a.claim_text: A Federal Reserve Board FEDS Note ('Monitoring AI Adoption in the U.S. Economy', Jeffrey S. Allen, April 3, 2026) synthesizing three US government/Fed surveys found: per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS), 18% of US firms had adopted AI by end of 2025; per the Real-Time Population Survey (RPS), 41% of the US workforce reported using generative AI at work as of November 2025; and per the Atlanta Fed's Survey of Business Uncertainty (SBU, Nov 2025, n=1,032 executives), 78% of the labor force works at an AI-adopting firm and 54% at a firm using large language models specifically; work-related generative AI adoption grew 31% year-over-year, with professional services (33%) and financial services (30%) leading sector adoption rates. This is firm/worker-level AI ADOPTION data, not evidence of productivity or employment effect.
claim_0da20db21fe1463a.scope: US firm and worker-level AI adoption rates (ADOPTION only -- not productivity or employment effect)
claim_0da20db21fe1463a.time_scope: Survey waves through November 2025; published April 3, 2026

claim_46bf083230ad547e.claim_text: Lightcast analysis of over 1.3 billion online job postings (report released July 23, 2025) found jobs requiring AI skills offer a 28% salary premium (approximately $18,000 more per year) compared to jobs without AI skill requirements, and that 51% of job postings requiring AI skills are now outside IT/computer-science occupations (spanning marketing/PR, HR, finance, science/research, and education/training), with generative-AI-related postings up roughly 800% in non-tech industries since 2022.
claim_46bf083230ad547e.scope: US job-postings-based wage premium for AI-skill requirements and cross-industry skill-demand diffusion; industry (vendor) analysis, not a peer-reviewed or government statistical study
claim_46bf083230ad547e.time_scope: Job postings data through mid-2025; published July 23, 2025
claim_46bf083230ad547e.geographic_scope: United States (Lightcast job postings database, primarily US-focused)
claim_46bf083230ad547e.created_from: O-2B WebFetch research (axis: wage evidence / skill demand evidence)

claim_67e1764a3b61ca91.claim_text: NBER Working Paper 33509 (Hampole, Papanikolaou, Schmidt, Seegmiller, "Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market", Feb 2025, revised Sept 2025), using NLP-measured task-level AI exposure across US firms and occupations 2010-2023, reports as descriptive (non-causal) evidence that a one-standard-deviation increase in firm-level AI utilization is associated with 11% higher average pay, consistent with AI-using firms being larger, more productive, and higher-paying than peers; the paper's main causal results concern labor demand/employment reallocation (AI-exposed tasks see reduced labor demand, offset by productivity-driven demand increases at adopting firms), not a causal wage-premium estimate by occupational AI exposure.
claim_67e1764a3b61ca91.scope: US firm-level correlation between AI utilization and average pay (descriptive only, not a causal AI wage-premium estimate); separately, firm-level labor demand/employment reallocation effects

claim_c195b340a92a8d90.claim_text: A Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta Workforce Currents report ("By Degree(s): Measuring Employer Demand for AI Skills by Educational Requirements", Sergio Galeano, Nyerere Hodge, and Alexander Ruder, published Aug 19, 2025), using Lightcast job-postings data from 2010-2024, finds that growth in employer demand for AI skills is not confined to bachelor's-degree occupations and is also appearing in job postings requiring only an associate degree or high school diploma, indicating AI-related skill demand is diffusing beyond traditionally higher-education-gated roles.
claim_c195b340a92a8d90.scope: US job-postings-based AI skill demand trend by required education level (qualitative diffusion finding; report does not provide the exact quantitative breakdown in the portion verified)
claim_c195b340a92a8d90.created_from: O-2B WebFetch research (axis: skill demand evidence)

claim_ea807921100c2653.claim_text: An ECB blog publication ("AI adoption and the productivity promise: what workers report", Aug 26, 2026), drawing on the ECB Consumer Expectations Survey of approximately 20,000 workers across 11 euro area countries, found AI use at work rose from 26% of workers in 2024 to 52% in 2026 (61% among highly educated workers vs. 37% among less educated), with adopters reporting median time-savings of about 3 hours/week (7.7% of median working time) and an estimated economy-wide efficiency gain of 3.8% when accounting for non-users; the survey found no evidence of AI reducing total employment at the firm level, though self-reported worker sentiment toward AI declined slightly (43% positive in the prior year to 41% in 2026).
claim_ea807921100c2653.scope: Euro area (11 countries) worker-reported AI adoption, time-savings/productivity, and firm-level employment effect (null employment effect); observed survey data

claim_cfb369e965025922.claim_text: Korea Employment Information Service (한국고용정보원) "2025-2035 Qualitative Job Outlook Report" (released May 18, 2026) qualitatively projects employment trends for 182 major domestic occupations through 2035 based on demographic (aging population), technological (AI/digital transformation), and cultural (K-content global expansion) factors; it forecasts approximately 93.4% of the 182 occupations will maintain current levels or increase (114 stable, 47 increasing slightly, 9 increasing), with no occupations forecast to decline -- this is a FORECAST/전망 of qualitative employment direction, not a measurement of AI-specific job losses or an observed outcome, and is Korea's official labor-market agency's outlook, separate from and less pessimistic in direction than KDI's AI-specific macroeconomic displacement forecast (claim_30fdf98bc1a9c818).
claim_cfb369e965025922.scope: Korea; national qualitative occupational outlook forecast (not AI-isolated; AI is one of several cited drivers) -- NOT an observed/realized outcome
claim_cfb369e965025922.created_from: O-2B WebFetch research (axis: Korea evidence beyond KDI)

claim_25cb5dc45e396783.claim_text: Axios reporting (Aug 19, 2025, citing Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee and labor-market data) on the 2025 US job-growth slowdown (3-month rolling average payroll growth falling from a peak of 548,000 in April 2022 to 35,000 by July 2025) attributes the slowdown primarily to non-AI factors: reduced immigration-driven labor supply (deportations, self-deportation, and workers avoiding workplaces amid immigration enforcement), demographic drag from baby boomers reaching retirement age, and employer hiring reluctance signaling demand-side economic weakness -- explicitly noting that reliable real-time immigration-flow data is unavailable, so the relative weight of each factor (including any AI contribution) cannot be precisely decomposed from current data.
claim_25cb5dc45e396783.scope: US aggregate labor market slowdown; alternative (non-AI) explanations -- immigration policy, demographics, cyclical hiring reluctance -- explicitly presented as competing with, and currently indistinguishable from, any AI-driven explanation

claim_1a69cf2e8f4f0f92.claim_text: Vanguard research (reported by Axios, Dec 17, 2025) analyzing nearly all US occupations using Labor Department occupational data from Q2 2023 to Q2 2025 found that occupations with the highest AI exposure experienced FASTER real wage growth (3.8% vs. 0.7% in less-exposed occupations) and FASTER employment growth (1.7% vs. 0.8%) over that period, counter to a mass-displacement narrative; Vanguard characterized this as "a snapshot of where we are now -- not a forecast of where we are headed," and separate reporting (CNN/ABC17, Dec 18, 2025) on related Vanguard analysis of ~140 AI-vulnerable occupations found high-AI-exposure jobs grew 1.7% post-Covid (mid-2023 to mid-2025) vs. 1% pre-Covid (2015-2019), with no systematic evidence of lower employment in AI-exposed roles, alongside isolated anecdotal Fed Beige Book reports of individual firms cutting staff or pausing entry-level hiring citing AI.
claim_1a69cf2e8f4f0f92.scope: US occupation-level observed employment and wage trends by AI exposure, Q2 2023-Q2 2025 -- counterevidence to a general AI-driven mass-displacement narrative (does not address the narrower early-career 22-25 cohort finding in claim_8fd5da8f27c9fc2b, which concerns a different, narrower population)
claim_1a69cf2e8f4f0f92.time_scope: Q2 2023 - Q2 2025 (and 2015-2019 pre-Covid baseline); published Dec 17-18, 2025
